subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Magnus effect explains how a spinning ball:
options: Swerves or dips because of a pressure difference created by the spin
questions.explain: Spin creates differing air velocities and pressures on each side of the ball (Magnus effect), producing a swerve or dip.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, the optimal angle of release to maximise horizontal distance when release and landing heights are equal is:
questions.explain: For equal release and landing heights with no air resistance, 45 degrees gives the greatest horizontal range.

questions.q: The net force acting on a body is:
options: The resultant of all forces acting on the body
The force of air resistance alone
questions.explain: Net (resultant) force is the overall vector sum of all forces acting on a body, determining its acceleration.

questions.q: Centre of mass is best described as:
options: The point at which the body's mass is evenly balanced in all directions
The lowest point of the body
The point where weight is zero
questions.explain: The centre of mass is the point about which the body's mass is balanced equally and through which weight acts.

questions.q: According to the Bernoulli principle, where air flows faster over a surface:
questions.explain: Bernoulli's principle states that faster-moving air exerts lower pressure, creating lift or directional forces.

questions.q: Newton's first law of motion applied to a stationary rugby ball states that the ball will:
options: Accelerate in the direction of net force
Remain at rest until acted on by an external (net) force
Exert an equal and opposite force on the ground
Move in a curved path due to spin
questions.explain: Newton's first law (inertia) states a body remains at rest, or in uniform motion, unless acted on by a net external force.

questions.q: Stability of a performer is increased by:
options: Lowering the centre of mass and widening the base of support
Moving the line of gravity outside the base
questions.explain: A lower centre of mass, a wider base and the line of gravity within the base all increase stability.

questions.q: Angular velocity is the rate of change of:
questions.explain: Angular velocity is angular displacement divided by the time taken, measured in radians per second.

questions.q: For a projectile such as a thrown javelin (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal velocity component is:
questions.explain: With no horizontal force (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal velocity component remains constant.

questions.q: Torque (the moment of a force) is calculated as:
options: Force × perpendicular distance from the axis
questions.explain: Torque, or moment, equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation.

questions.q: The vertical velocity component of a projectile at the highest point of its flight is:
questions.explain: At the peak of flight the vertical velocity is momentarily zero before gravity accelerates the object downwards.

questions.q: Newton's second law of motion is expressed as:
questions.explain: Newton's second law states that force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (F = ma), or rate of change of momentum.

questions.q: Velocity differs from speed because velocity is:
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector — displacement divided by time — possessing both magnitude and direction, unlike scalar speed.

questions.q: A figure skater pulls in their arms during a spin and speeds up. This demonstrates that, with angular momentum conserved:
options: Decreasing moment of inertia increases angular velocity
Increasing moment of inertia increases angular velocity
Angular velocity is independent of body shape
questions.explain: With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved; reducing moment of inertia increases angular velocity.

questions.q: For a body to remain balanced, its line of gravity must fall:
options: At the highest point of the body
questions.explain: Balance is maintained while the line of gravity passes through the base of support.

questions.q: Impulse is correctly defined as:
options: Force × time, equal to the change in momentum
questions.explain: Impulse equals force multiplied by the time it acts, and equals the change in momentum it produces.

questions.q: Moment of inertia depends on a body's mass and:
options: The distribution of mass relative to the axis of rotation
questions.explain: Moment of inertia is determined by mass and how that mass is distributed about the axis of rotation.

questions.q: Momentum is calculated as:
questions.explain: Linear momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity.

questions.q: On a force-time graph for a foot strike in running, a net positive impulse indicates the runner is:
questions.explain: A net positive impulse means a net forward force over time, increasing momentum and accelerating the runner.

questions.q: A first-class lever in the body has the:
options: Fulcrum between the effort and the load
questions.explain: A first-class lever has the fulcrum between the effort and the load, as at the elbow during extension or the neck.

questions.q: A long jumper increasing the time over which the take-off force is applied will, for a given force:
options: Increase the change in momentum and so the velocity at take-off
questions.explain: By the impulse-momentum relationship, a larger impulse (force × time) produces a greater change in momentum and velocity.

questions.q: Conservation of angular momentum applies while a gymnast is airborne because:
options: The moment of inertia is fixed
No external torque acts about the centre of mass
questions.explain: In flight, gravity acts through the centre of mass producing no torque, so angular momentum stays constant.

questions.q: Most levers in the human body are third-class, which means they:
options: Have the load in the middle
Sacrifice force but favour speed and range of movement
questions.explain: Third-class levers have the effort between fulcrum and load, giving a mechanical disadvantage but greater speed and range.

questions.q: A sprinter pushing back and down on the blocks, and being driven forwards and up, best illustrates Newton's:
questions.explain: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, generating the ground reaction force.

questions.q: Weight as a force acts:
options: Vertically downwards through the centre of mass
Horizontally in the direction of motion
Perpendicular to the reaction force only
questions.explain: Weight is the gravitational force acting vertically downwards through a body's centre of mass.

questions.q: Three factors that determine the horizontal distance of a projectile are speed of release, angle of release and:
questions.explain: Speed of release, angle of release and height of release together determine the horizontal distance travelled.

questions.q: Drag (fluid friction) acting on a cyclist is reduced by:
questions.explain: A streamlined position reduces frontal surface area and turbulence, lowering air resistance (drag).

questions.q: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of:
questions.explain: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time (change in velocity ÷ time taken).

questions.q: Friction is increased by:
options: Reducing the mass of the body
A larger normal reaction force pressing the surfaces together
questions.explain: Friction increases with a greater normal reaction force and rougher surfaces, improving grip and traction.

questions.q: A second-class lever always provides a mechanical advantage because:
options: The fulcrum is in the middle
The effort arm is shorter than the load arm
The effort arm is longer than the load (resistance) arm
questions.explain: In a second-class lever the effort arm exceeds the load arm, so a small effort moves a large load — a mechanical advantage.
